title: Devilled Mackerel
subtitle: Grilled mackerel fillets in a hot mustard and cayenne glaze
excerpt: Fresh mackerel fillets grilled with a pungent glaze of English mustard, cayenne, Worcestershire sauce, and a little butter. A quick, bold-flavoured British supper ready in 15 minutes.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Devilled fish as a category; mackerel is listed as a common candidate for devilling. Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845), devilled preparations for oily fish. English mustard and cayenne are the traditional British devilling agents.

content.text: Devilled mackerel is fresh mackerel fillets grilled under a high heat with a spiced mustard glaze. The glaze takes 2 minutes to mix; the fish takes 8 minutes under the grill. Mackerel handles the aggressive seasoning well because the fish itself is rich and oily. The result is emphatically flavoured in a way that is distinctly British: hot, sharp, savoury.

items.prepNote: half for the glaze, half to serve

content.text: Heat the grill to its highest setting. Line a baking tray with foil.

Mix {{english-mustard}} of English mustard, {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce, {{cayenne-pepper}} of cayenne, {{unsalted-butter}} of melted butter. Add the juice of half the {{lemon}}. Mix well.
Score the skin of each mackerel fillet 3 or 4 times with a sharp knife. Lay the fillets skin-side up on the tray. Spoon the glaze over the skin and into the cuts.
Grill for 6 to 8 minutes until the glaze is catching and the fish is cooked through. The flesh should flake easily when pressed. Serve with the remaining lemon cut into wedges.

rows.symptom: Glaze burns before fish is cooked
rows.cause: Grill too close to the element
rows.fix: Position the tray about 10 cm below the grill element, not directly under it.

rows.symptom: Fish is dry and flakes apart
rows.fix: Mackerel is done when the flesh just turns opaque and parts easily. 6 to 8 minutes under a high grill is usually enough.
Devilled preparations should be distinctly spicy. Add more cayenne and mustard. The richness of the mackerel absorbs seasoning well.

rows.cause: Skin not scored or moisture on the surface
rows.fix: Pat the skin dry with kitchen paper before applying the glaze. Score it so the heat reaches the flesh and the skin can contract.

content.text: Devilling meat and fish was popular in British cooking throughout the nineteenth century. It meant grilling with mustard, cayenne, and strong sauces. Devilled kidneys, devilled bones, and devilled fish all appear in Victorian cookbooks of the period. Mackerel suits this treatment well. Its oily richness carries strong seasoning that would overwhelm a leaner white fish.
